content: The decision to collect specimens for pathological examination is made by physicians or nurses who possess specialized knowledge of the disease and the appropriate sampling methods. Incorrect sampling techniques can lead to suboptimal specimen collection, which may adversely affect the accuracy of the final diagnosis. Examples of sampling methods and their corresponding sites include the following: Surgical specimens: Core needle biopsy (e.g., bone marrow, breast), endoscopic biopsy (e.g., nose, sinus, gastrointestinal tract, bronchus, lung), minimally invasive surgical biopsy (e.g., thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic organs), and surgical resection (any organ). Cytology specimens: Smears (e.g., cervix, vagina, vulva, gastrointestinal tract, pulmonary system, skin), body fluids (e.g., urine, sputum, bronchial washings, cerebrospinal fluid, pleural, peritoneal, pericardial, synovial fluids), and aspirates (e.g., bone marrow, tumors, radiology-guided or blind). Specimens should generally be fixed to preserve their state as close to the living condition as possible, preventing shrinkage, autolysis, or bacterial degradation. Different fixatives may be required for specialized studies. Proper labeling of specimens is critical. Labels must include patient identification (e.g., name, hospital number), sampling site, and the date and time of collection. Labels should be affixed to the primary container, not the lid, and specimens from different sites or lesions must be submitted in separate containers. A pathology request form must be completed with all relevant information, such as patient details, clinical history, sampling site, and requested tests. Incomplete forms may result in specimen rejection. Providing comprehensive clinical data to the pathologist is essential, and direct communication or shared electronic medical records can facilitate this process. Specimens are often transported from distant healthcare facilities to pathology laboratories for processing and testing. During transport, proper handling is crucial to maintain specimen integrity. Specimens must be labeled correctly and fixed appropriately upon receipt at the laboratory. Real-time tracking of specimen movement ensures accurate documentation and operational efficiency. Pre-determined rejection criteria for specimens (e.g., unlabeled specimens, insufficient patient information, mismatched labels) must be communicated to all clinicians and facilities. Upon arrival at the laboratory, specimens and request forms are matched for identifiers. Once verified, specimens are accessioned and assigned a unique pathology number for tracking throughout processing. Barcoded labels enhance efficiency and accuracy by enabling real-time tracking of all case components (e.g., tissue blocks, slides, stains). For surgical specimens, gross examination involves describing, measuring, and dissecting the specimen to fit into tissue cassettes for processing. The description includes color, shape, texture, and dimensions. Large specimens requiring dissection should have detailed documentation of findings and cassette contents. Tissue processing, from formalin fixation to paraffin embedding, is best performed using automated tissue processors. Thin sections (5–6 microns) are cut using a microtome, floated on a warm water bath, and mounted onto glass slides. Cytology specimens, such as liquid-based cytology, require centrifugation or filtration to separate cells. These cells are then deposited onto glass slides as a thin layer through sedimentation or pressure application. Staining is necessary for microscopic examination. Routine histopathology uses hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, while special stains and immunohistochemical stains are employed when additional information is required. After staining, slides are dehydrated, mounted with media, and covered with thin glass to create permanent preparations. Stained slides are assembled with request forms for pathologist review. Pathology reports must be comprehensive, accurate, and adhere to established guidelines. They should include diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive information based on the specimen type. Synoptic reporting, a structured documentation method, ensures consistency, reduces errors, and improves patient care. Benefits include faster turnaround times, elimination of transcription costs, streamlined report distribution, and more complete and interpretable reports. Specimen retention policies must comply with national regulations. Tissue blocks and slides are typically retained for at least 10 years, while remnant tissue may be discarded 30 days after the case is officially signed out. Patient data and reports should be archived permanently, with access restricted to authorized personnel to maintain confidentiality. When establishing a pathology laboratory, a situation analysis of national policies, regulatory frameworks, and service needs is essential. Stakeholder engagement, including hospital management and laboratory staff, is critical. Laboratories should be integrated into a tiered network, with national reference laboratories supporting regional and district facilities. Proper infrastructure, equipment, and resource allocation are necessary for efficient and safe laboratory operations.
